title: The choice of cranial window type for _in vivo_ imaging significantly affects dendritic spine turnover in the cortex
protocol: Anesthetize transgenic mice by intraperitoneal injection of 0.2 ml/20 g body weight of a mixture containing 20 mg/ml Ketamine and 3 mg/ml Xylazine in 0.9% NaCl.
Thoroughly shave the hair over most of the scalp with a conventional razor blade.
Perform a midline scalp incision using microsurgical tools, extending approximately from the neck region to the frontal area.
Remove soft tissue attached to the skull over the area to be imaged with fine forceps.
High-speed micro-drill is used to thin a circular area of skull typically ~1 mm in diameter over the region of interest under a dissection microscope.
Drilling should be done intermittently and the drill bit can be immersed periodically in cold artificial cerebrospinal fluid (ACSF) solution to minimize heat-induced tissue injury.
Remove the external compact bone layer from the mouse skull.
Thin the middle layer of spongy bone to about 75% of its original thickness.
Continue until concentric cavities within the spongy bone become visible under the dissecting microscope.
Ensure that the remaining skull thickness is more than 50 μm.
Glue three razor blades together to form a metal plate for immobilizing the skull.
Apply a small amount of cyanoacrylate glue around the edges of the internal opening of the blade.
Press the blade against the mouse skull, leaving the imaging area uncovered and surrounded by the internal blade opening.
Wait 10–15 minutes until the metal plate is firmly glued to the skull.
Place the mouse face down with the blades supported by the acrylic blocks.
Tighten up the screws to completely immobilize the blades.
Wash the area to be imaged extensively with ACSF to remove remnants of non-polymerized glue.
Use a microsurgical blade to thin a smaller area less than 200 μm in diameter to 20 μm in thickness.
Shave the bone using the blade at a 45-degree angle carefully.
Continue thinning until a very thin (20 μm) and smooth preparation (~200 μm in diameter) is achieved.
Determine the optimal degree of skull thinning by visualizing dendrites and spines with a conventional fluorescence microscope.
Anesthetize transgenic mice and shave the hair over most of the scalp.
Administer dexamethasone by intramuscular injection (0.02 ml at 4 mg/ml).
Remove soft tissue attached to the skull over the area to be imaged with fine forceps.
Use a high-speed micro-drill to thin a circumference of a 5 x 5 mm region of the skull over the region of interest under a dissection microscope.
Lift up the island of bone within the drilled circle with a pair of sharp forceps.
Rinse the cortex with room temperature ACSF once or twice if necessary.
Cover the clear dura with a thin layer of low-melting-point agarose (1.2% in ACSF).
Gently lower a custom-made circular coverslip (5–7 mm diameter, No. 1 thickness) onto the open-skull region.
Remove any excess agarose with sterile cotton applicators.
Seal the edge of the optical window to the skull with a thin layer of cyanoacrylate glue.
Cover all exposed areas of the skull and embed a small custom-made steel bar into dental acrylic for stabilization.
Allow mice to recover 7–14 days before starting chronic imaging.
Obtain a high-quality picture of meningeal blood vessels using a CCD camera attached to a stereo dissecting microscope as a landmark for relocation.
Place the mouse under an epi-fluorescence microscope and select a specific area for two-photon imaging.
Carefully identify the selected area in the CCD camera map by observing the pattern of brain vasculature adjacent to it.
Mark the identified area on the map.
Tune the TPM to the appropriate wavelength (e.g., 920 nm for YFP).
Use ACSF for objective immersion throughout imaging.
Obtain a stack of fluorescently labeled neuronal processes at a digital zoom of 1x.
Take a zoomed image of the same area without changing the stage position (e.g., 3x zoom).
Typically, the stack depth is 100 μm below the pial surface.
Use laser intensities in the range of 10 to 20 milliwatts measured at the sample to minimize phototoxicity.
Obtain additional zoomed images around the central image by moving the imaging position electronically 360° around the initial imaged area.
Detach the head immobilization device gently from the skull with thinned-skull preparations.
Suture the scalp with 6-0 silk suture.
Keep the mouse in a separate cage until fully awake.
Return the mouse to the original cage after it is fully awake.
Dismount the steel bar from the fixing post for open skull preparations.
